# Results — Study 623 (IPO Long-Run Underperformance)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test
(Ritter 1991; Loughran & Ritter 1995; Ritter & Welch 2002) — **IPOs underperform seasoned
stocks for 3-5 years after listing: the first-day pop is for the flippers, the multi-year
drift is for the bagholders** — tested on two tracks: (A) Ritter's published cohort table
(1980-2024, hardcoded from his April 2026 update, source PDF cached) re-run through our
Newey-West framing, and (B) the live, investable tape: Renaissance IPO ETF monthly total
returns vs SPY/IWM/IWO, Nov 2013 → Jun 2026. Offline & deterministic once cached; run
`python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30** (the last
complete calendar month; the partial current month is dropped). Fingerprint `65b022ff4f0e`.*

## Data stamp

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Track A | Ritter, *IPOs: Updated Long-run Statistics*, **Table 19** (updated 2026-02-16): 45 cohort years 1980-2024, **9,253 IPOs**, avg 3-yr buy-and-hold returns from the first close, raw / market-adjusted (CRSP VW) / style-adjusted (size+B/M matched seasoned firms). Hardcoded in `data.py` with the source URL; PDF cached in `_cache/`. 2023-24 cohorts are truncated windows (returns through 2025-12-31). |
| Track B | yfinance daily adjusted (total-return, net-of-fee) closes: **IPO** (Renaissance IPO ETF, inception 2013-10-16), **SPY**, **IWM**, **IWO** (Russell 2000 Growth = small-growth style benchmark), **^IRX** (13-wk T-bill, the risk-free leg). 2013-11-30 → 2026-06-30, **152 months (12.7 years)**. |
| Inference | Newey-West HAC *t* everywhere: lag 6 on the monthly ETF series; lag 3 across cohort years (consecutive cohorts hold overlapping 3-year windows — serially correlated by construction). |
| Execution / costs | The claim is a *passive holding* claim — no signal to lag: the rule is calendar-known (always-on $1/$1 spread, monthly re-hedge), effective lag **zero by construction, documented**. Tradable expression = short IPO ETF / long SPY: short leg pays **1-2%/yr borrow** (charged monthly), **5/10 bps one-way × NAV** on the re-hedge turnover, both legs counted. ETF expense ratios are already inside the adjusted NAV tape. Spreads are self-financing, so races are excess-vs-excess by construction. |
| Survivorship | Neither track is survivor-biased: Ritter's table follows every IPO to its delisting date, and the ETF's index return already nets holdings that crater. The live track's real caveat is **regime coverage**, not survivorship: 2013+ misses the 1980-2000 cohorts where the drag was largest. |

## Track A — Ritter's published cohort record, through our stats (literature track)

One observation per cohort year (equal-weighted mean 3-yr BHAR), NW *t* across 45 cohorts:

| adjustment | mean %/3yr | NW *t* | N-weighted | cohorts negative |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| raw (absolute) | **+22.50%** | **+3.20** | +19.13% | 22.2% |
| **market-adjusted (CRSP VW)** | **−14.20%** | **−2.26** | −20.51% | **71.1%** |
| style-adjusted (size+B/M match) | **−8.46%** | **−1.52** | −8.87% | 66.7% |

Dropping the truncated 2023-24 cohorts: market-adjusted **−12.03% (t = −2.18)**,
style-adjusted **−6.60% (t = −1.37)**. Ritter's own aggregate row: 9,253 IPOs, first-day
**+18.9%**, 3-yr raw +19.1%, market-adjusted **−20.5%**, style-adjusted **−8.9%**.

The published record does show the drift — the market-adjusted cohort mean clears |t| ≥ 2
(−2.26). But **Ritter's own style adjustment kills the significance** (t = −1.52): most of
the "IPO effect" is the small-growth clothes IPOs wear. And by desk law, a published,
pre-aggregated table is the **literature story, never the REAL stamp** — the stamp is
earned (or not) by the investable tape below.

## Track B — the live tape (the judge): Renaissance IPO ETF, 2013-11 → 2026-06

Growth of $1 (total return): **IPO 3.10× (+9.34%/yr)** vs **SPY 5.27× (+14.02%/yr)**,
IWM 3.25× (+9.74%/yr), IWO 3.37× (+10.07%/yr). The IPO/SPY relative line peaked at
**1.45×** (2021-01), ends at **0.59×** — a **−67.5%** relative drawdown — yet IPO beats SPY
in exactly **50.0%** of months.

| benchmark | spread (bps/mo) | ann. | HAC *t* | alpha (bps/mo) | ann. | HAC *t* | beta |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **vs SPY** | −16.36 | −1.95%/yr | **−0.31** | −46.71 | −5.46%/yr | **−0.99** | 1.293 |
| vs IWM | +8.39 | +1.01%/yr | +0.17 | +8.86 | +1.07%/yr | +0.18 | 0.994 |
| **vs IWO (small growth)** | +4.79 | +0.58%/yr | +0.12 | **+0.23** | **+0.03%/yr** | **+0.01** | 1.055 |
| two-factor (SPY + IWO−SPY spread) | | | | −4.66 | −0.56%/yr | **−0.12** | mkt 1.091 · style 0.999 |

The live tape does **not** clear the bar: the vs-SPY CAPM alpha is −46.71 bps/mo
(−5.46%/yr) at **HAC t = −0.99** — a drag-shaped point estimate, nowhere near significance.
And the moment the benchmark matches the style (IWO, or the two-factor model with a
**0.999** loading on the small-growth spread), the alpha collapses to **≈ 0** (t = +0.01 /
−0.12). On the investable tape, "recent IPOs" behaved like a leveraged small-growth basket
(beta 1.29 on SPY), not like a cursed asset class.

## Tradability — shorting the drift (net of borrow + costs)

Always-on short-IPO / long-SPY $1/$1 spread, monthly re-hedge, borrow charged monthly on
the short leg, one-way costs × NAV on the re-hedge turnover (both legs):

| one-way cost | borrow | gross (bps/mo) | net (bps/mo) | net ann. | HAC *t* | max drawdown |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5 bps | 1%/yr | +16.36 (t = +0.31) | **+7.63** | **+0.92%/yr** | +0.15 | **−57.4%** |
| 10 bps | 1%/yr | +16.36 | +7.23 | +0.87%/yr | +0.14 | −57.5% |
| 5 bps | 2%/yr | +16.36 | **−0.70** | **−0.08%/yr** | −0.01 | −59.5% |

A statistically empty ~+0.9%/yr that **goes negative at 2%/yr borrow** and rode through a
**−57%** drawdown when IPOs melted up into early 2021. The zero-cost version of the claim
("just don't buy IPOs early") costs nothing but also *earns* nothing reliable vs simply
owning a small-growth fund. **Mirage.**

## Synthetic control — the machinery is faithful (and the power is known)

Deterministic synthetic worlds (planted monthly alpha on a beta-1.25 IPO leg), HAC-alpha
detector, **averaged over 20 seeds** (desk law — no single-seed baselines):

| planted alpha | measured (bps/mo) | mean HAC *t* | \|t\| ≥ 2 rejection rate |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| **0 bps/mo (null)** | +6.31 | +0.21 | **5%** (nominal) |
| −50 bps/mo (Ritter-sized) | −43.69 | −1.83 | 45% |
| −100 bps/mo (large) | −93.69 | −3.88 | **95%** |

The detector is unbiased (null rejects at exactly the nominal 5%) and recovers planted
drags. **Power note, stated honestly:** a Ritter-sized −50 bps/mo drag is detected only
~45% of the time in a 152-month window — the live tape could miss a modest true drag. But
the style-adjusted evidence (both Ritter's own table and the live two-factor alpha of
−0.12 t) says whatever drag exists is mostly *style*, not IPO-ness. *(The synthetic control
is a machinery/power proof only — never cited in support of a stamp.)*

## Verdict

- **Signal — WEAK.** The literature record is real: across 45 published cohort years the
  market-adjusted 3-yr drift is **−14.20%/3yr at NW t = −2.26** (N-weighted −20.5%), 71% of
  cohorts negative. But (a) **Ritter's own style adjustment drops it to t = −1.52**, and
  (b) on our live, investable tape (152 months of the Renaissance IPO ETF) the vs-SPY alpha
  is **t = −0.99** and the style-matched alpha is **≈ 0** — the tape alone cannot certify
  the drift. The literature says real; this tape can't — **WEAK**, per the inference bar.
  (No survivorship bias on either track; the live window's regime coverage — 2013+ only —
  is the named caveat.)
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** Shorting the drift nets a statistically empty **+0.92%/yr**
  (t = +0.15) at 5 bps + 1% borrow, **goes negative at 2% borrow**, and carried a **−57%**
  drawdown through the 2020 IPO melt-up. Nothing deployable survives.
- **Third axis — "Is it small-growth beta rather than IPO-ness?" — CONFIRMED.** Ritter's
  own style adjustment cuts the cohort drag from −14.20% (t = −2.26) to −8.46%
  (t = −1.52, insignificant); on the live tape the −5.46%/yr vs-SPY alpha collapses to
  **+0.03%/yr vs IWO** and **−0.56%/yr (t = −0.12)** in the two-factor model, with a
  **0.999** loading on the small-growth spread. The bagholder's real mistake is buying
  *expensive small-growth exposure* — the IPO wrapper is mostly incidental.
